label: thm:mainSO3
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mainSO3}
Assume \eqref{eq:H}, $G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and $X\cong S^3$. Every singular isotropy group is $T$, and the number $r$ of singular orbits satisfies $1\le r\le3$ and $\chi(M)=2r$. The abstract weighted graph $\Sigma$ is one of the nine families in Tables~\ref{tab:graphs} and \ref{tab:lollislices}.

If every exceptional isotropy group is cyclic, then $r=2$ or $3$. For $r=2$ the action is equivariantly diffeomorphic to
\[
 N^G_{p,q}=G\times_T S(\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb C_p\oplus\mathbb C_q),
 \qquad p,q\ge1,\quad\gcd(p,q)=1,
\]
and $M\cong S^2\times S^4$. For $r=3$ it is equivariantly diffeomorphic to
\[
 P_{a,b}=G\times_T\mathbb{CP}^2
 =\mathbb P(\mathbf 1\oplus L^{2a}\oplus L^{2(a+b)})\longrightarrow S^2,
 \qquad a,b\ge1,\quad\gcd(a,b)=1,
\]
where $c_1(L)$ generates $H^2(S^2)$. The underlying manifold is the product $S^2\times\mathbb{CP}^2$ precisely when $a\equiv b\pmod3$; otherwise it is the nontrivial unoriented diffeomorphism type of a linear $\mathbb{CP}^2$-bundle over $S^2$.

The remaining graphs are a dihedral $Y$, five types of lollipop, and one $D_3$--$A_4$ theta graph. Their rational intersection forms and Pontryagin covectors are given in Section~\ref{sec:branchinvariants}. The nine-family list is necessary; it is not a positive-curvature realization theorem or a classification of all spatial embeddings.
head: environment
name: $\SO(3)$ and a spherical quotient

label: thm:mainball
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mainball}
Assume \eqref{eq:H}, $G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$, and $X\cong B^3$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item In Liu's Figure~2(b), the underlying manifold is
\[
 E_n=S(\xi_n)\longrightarrow S^4,\qquad p_1(\xi_n)=4n u,
 \qquad n\in\mathbb Z,
\]
where $\xi_n$ is an oriented three-plane bundle and $u$ generates $H^4(S^4)$. The ordinary diffeomorphism type is determined by $|n|$; $E_0=S^2\times S^4$ and $E_1=\mathbb{CP}^3$.
\item In Figure~2(c), the smooth action is obtained by gluing a weight-$(1,1)$ singular-orbit tube to a two-disk bundle over $S^2\times S^2$ whose Euler class is $2a+kb$. The gluing exists exactly for odd $k$ and has no further equivariant attaching parameter. The resulting manifolds $M_k$ satisfy
\[
 M_k\cong M_\ell\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |k|=|\ell|.
\]
They are non-spin, have torsion-free homology, and their full cubic and Pontryagin data are given in \eqref{eq:Mkcubic}--\eqref{eq:Mkp1}.
\item Figure~2(e) cannot occur. More generally, if $f$ is the number of isolated boundary fixed points with tangent representation $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3$, and $r$ is the number of interior singular points, then $f+2r\le3$.
\item In Figure~2(f), $M$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{CP}^3$. The known projective $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ action realizes this configuration with positive curvature.
\end{enumerate}
Figures~2(a) and~2(d) are the cases treated by Liu; in~(d) the underlying manifold is diffeomorphic, not merely homeomorphic, to the standard $S^6$. The smooth families in (i)--(ii) do not assert positive-curvature realizability for every parameter.
head: environment
name: $\SO(3)$ and a ball quotient

label: thm:mainSU2
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: $\SU(2)$ and a spherical quotient

label: cor:globalelliptic
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:globalelliptic}
Every manifold satisfying \eqref{eq:H} is rationally elliptic. In particular,
\[
 H^{\mathrm{odd}}(M;\mathbb Q)=0,\qquad
 b_2(M)=b_4(M)=\frac{\chi(M)-2}{2}\le2.
\]
The possible real homotopy types are $S^6$, $\mathbb{CP}^3$, $S^2\times S^4$, $S^2\times\mathbb{CP}^2$, $F_{\mathrm W}$, and $\mathbb{CP}^3\#\mathbb{CP}^3$.
head: environment

label: lem:extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:extension}
For the tubes in \eqref{eq:tubetrivial}, every $G$-equivariant diffeomorphism of $B^G_{p,q}$ is equivariantly isotopic to the restriction of a diffeomorphism of $U^G_{p,q}$. In particular, the isotopy itself can be absorbed in a collar, so an attaching map to such a tube introduces no additional parameter once the other piece and its boundary identification have been fixed.
head: environment
name: Equivariant boundary extension

title: Proof
body_md:
The boundary is a locally free $G$-space over $S^2(p,q)$. An induced quotient diffeomorphism preserves the cone orders. An orientation-preserving orbifold diffeomorphism of this sphere is isotopic to the identity: remove invariant disks at its at most two cone points, use the marked version of the sphere isotopy theorem \cite{Smale}, and perform the isotopy in the cyclic disk charts. There are no two distinct equal nontrivial orders, since $\gcd(p,q)=1$. Lifting this isotopy with an invariant connection reduces the problem to an equivariant map over the identity.

Such maps are sections of the adjoint orbibundle. In a chart with isotropy $C_m$, the value at the chart center lies in its centralizer. For $G=\mathrm{SU}(2)$, every nontrivial $m$ here is odd and its centralizer is a connected circle. Move these values to the identity through their centralizers. Obstruction theory on the remaining two-dimensional orbifold charts now reduces the section to the identity: $\pi_1(\mathrm{SU}(2))=\pi_2(\mathrm{SU}(2))=0$.

For $G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$ one must account for the disconnected centralizer of a half-turn. Consider the fiberwise double cover of the adjoint bundle with fiber $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. The obstruction to lifting a section is a class in
\[
 H^1_{\mathrm{orb}}(S^2(p,q);\mathbb Z/2)=0.
\]
Indeed the orbifold fundamental group has presentation
$\langle a,b\mid a^p=b^q=ab=1\rangle$ and is cyclic of order $\gcd(p,q)=1$. This also shows why a value in a disconnected half-turn centralizer cannot be chosen independently at a cone point. A lifted section has its values in the centralizers of the lifted cyclic subgroups of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, which are connected. The preceding contraction and the same vanishing homotopy groups apply. This is the usual obstruction-theoretic description of orbibundle gauge sections; see \cite{AdemLeidaRuan} for the orbifold bundle language.

It remains to treat quotient orientation reversal. Let $w\in N_G(T)\setminus T$ and let $c$ be complex conjugation on both weight summands. Since $c(t v)=t^{-1}c(v)$ and $wtw^{-1}=t^{-1}$, the map
\[
 [g,v]\longmapsto[gw,c(v)]
\]
is a well-defined equivariant diffeomorphism of the whole tube. It reverses the orientation of its spindle quotient. Composing with it reduces the remaining case to the orientation-preserving one. The isotopies constructed above extend across an invariant collar. Smoothness at a cyclic chart center follows by working equivariantly in the covering disk throughout.
head: environment

label: lem:normal
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Normal characters

title: Proof
body_md: At a principal orbit $G/C_m$ the two endpoint representations restrict to the same complex character, which is exactly $u\equiv v\pmod m$. The normal bundle can be constructed on the two cohomogeneity-one disk bundles over the sections using these characters. On their common principal orbit any two complex-linear intertwiners differ by an element of $\mathbb C^*$, a connected group. Thus no additional clutching component remains. The restrictions to the sections have Chern numbers $d_Gu,d_Gv$, and \eqref{eq:sections} gives the fiber evaluation. Conversely these constructions realize every compatible pair. Since $A_m$ is simply connected, the homotopy sequence of its oriented circle bundle identifies its fundamental group with $\mathbb Z$ modulo the image of evaluation by $e(\nu)$. The section and fiber form an integral basis of $H_2(A_m)$, proving \eqref{eq:primitive}.
head: environment

label: prop:localization
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply the equivariant localization theorem \cite{AB,BV}; only its specialization needs explanation. Since $H^j(B\mathrm{SU}(2);\mathbb Z)=0$ for $1\le j\le3$, every degree-two class has a unique $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-equivariant lift. At the two circle-fixed points of $S_i$, the lift restricts to $n_i(x)t$ and $-n_i(x)t$, where $t$ generates $H^2(BT)$. The tangent weights for this circle are
\[
 2,\ d_Gp_i,\ d_Gq_i.
\]
Their Euler products are $2\varepsilon_i d_G^2p_iq_i t^3$ and its negative, while the equivariant first Pontryagin class is
$(4+d_G^2p_i^2+d_G^2q_i^2)t^2$ at either point. Applying localization to $x$, to $xyz$, and to $p_1x$ gives \eqref{eq:lin}--\eqref{eq:pon}. The integration of the degree-two lift is zero for dimensional reasons.

Equation~\eqref{eq:betti} gives equivariant formality over $\mathbb Q$. Restriction of equivariant cohomology to the circle-fixed set is therefore injective. If all $n_i(x)$ vanish, the unique equivariant lift vanishes and so does $x$. The image has dimension $b_2=r-1$, which proves the hyperplane assertion.
head: environment

label: lem:connected
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:connected}
Every singular isotropy group is $T=\mathrm{SO}(2)$. Its normal slice is $\mathbb C_p\oplus\mathbb C_q$ with nonzero coprime weights. If $r$ denotes the number of singular orbits, then
\[
 1\le r\le3,\qquad \chi(M)=2r.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fixed points would lie in the boundary of the quotient, by the six-dimensional fixed-point representations listed by Liu. A remaining singular isotropy group is $T$ or its normalizer $\mathrm O(2)$. At an interior isolated singular orbit both circle weights on the four-dimensional slice are nonzero. An element of $\mathrm O(2)\setminus T$ conjugates the circle to its inverse. On the slice it is anti-complex-linear on two complex dimensions, hence has positive real determinant, including when the two weights have equal absolute value. On the tangent plane of $G/\mathrm O(2)=\mathbb{RP}^2$ it reverses orientation. It would therefore reverse the orientation of $M$. This is impossible for an element of the connected group $G$.

Thus every singular orbit is $G/T$. Slice effectiveness and trivial principal isotropy give $\gcd(p,q)=1$, while a zero weight would produce a boundary face. Every singular sphere contains two $T$-fixed points and no principal or exceptional orbit contains any. The Euler formula and singular-orbit bound of Liu now give the result.
head: environment

label: lem:edgecong
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:edgecong}
For an order-$m$ edge, the endpoint transverse characters satisfy $u\equiv\pm v\pmod m$. The only ambiguity in comparing the characters is inversion, not multiplication by an arbitrary unit of $\mathbb Z/m$.
head: environment
name: Edge congruence

title: Proof
body_md: Along a connected open edge, its normal slice representation is locally constant after identifying its isotropy subgroup. Conjugation in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ between two identifications of a rotation subgroup is induced by an element of its normalizer and acts on the rotation circle by identity or inversion. Restricting the endpoint slice to this subgroup gives the asserted congruence.
head: environment

label: prop:graphlist
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:graphlist}
The graph $\Sigma$, after forgetting its embedding in $S^3$, belongs to exactly one family in Table~\ref{tab:graphs}, up to graph isomorphism and the indicated parameter symmetries.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We start with the eighteen graphs of \cite[Proposition 5.1]{KSR}. The specialization is explicit: graphs $1,2,3$ there are the cases with no edges; graphs $4,5,6,8,9$ give II, IV, VII, III, V; graphs $7,18$ contain a one-vertex loop; graphs $10,12,13,15,16$ have a three-valent non-orbifold vertex; graph $11$ gives VIII, graph $14$ the subdivided theta, and graph $17$ the point-plus-interval. A non-orbifold vertex here has circle isotropy and valency at most two, so the five three-valent cases are impossible. A one-vertex loop of order $m>1$ would force the slice pair $(m,m)$, contrary to coprimality.

For a path order its labels $a<b$. At the order-$b$ edge, the endpoint transverse characters are $1,a$, so $a\equiv\pm1\pmod b$. With $a\ge2$, this gives $a=b-1$. For a genuine triangle let $a<b<c$ be its labels. Along the $c$ edge, $a\equiv\pm b\pmod c$. The positive sign is impossible and the negative sign gives $c=a+b$. These are IV and V.

The global graph theorem gives an order-two edge on the cycle of a lollipop. Write its other cycle order as $k$ and its stem order as $\ell$. Coprimality at the cycle's circle vertex forces $k$ odd. Substitution of $(2,k,\ell)$ in the four finite-slice triples gives precisely Table~\ref{tab:lollislices}. Comparing the transverse character $2$ on the order-$k$ edge and the character $1$ on the stem gives the last column. The same comparison at the order-$m$ leaf of a $Y$ forces its finite-slice weight to be $\pm1$.

For the theta reduction we use the exceptional-track obstruction of \cite[Lemma 2.10]{KSR}. A complete quotient geodesic track that continues through finite vertices cannot avoid every singular vertex. In a finite slice, continuation pairs antipodal axis directions. At $D_m$, the two order-two arms are interchanged when $m$ is odd, while all arms reflect individually when $m$ is even. At $A_4$ the two order-three arms are interchanged and the order-two arm reflects. At $S_4$ and $A_5$ every arm reflects. These statements follow directly from the rotation-axis orbits on the unit two-sphere.

Let the two direct edges of a subdivided theta have orders $r,q$. If both are order two, they form a finite-only track, whether the endpoints interchange or reflect them. If they have different orders, a direct arm reflected at both endpoints likewise gives a forbidden track. The only available interchange mechanisms are the order-two pair at an odd dihedral vertex and the order-three pair at a tetrahedral vertex. Both must occur. Thus the direct orders are $2,3$, the finite vertices are $D_3,A_4$, and the remaining arms have orders $2,3$ and meet at the sole circle vertex. This gives IX.

Two topological restrictions complete the argument. If there are no edges, all slices are $(1,1)$. Remove $r$ tubes $U^G_{1,1}$. The remainder is a principal $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ bundle over $S^3$ with $r$ open balls removed. Each boundary restriction has nonzero $w_2$, because its total space $S^2\times S^3$ is simply connected. The sum of the boundary sphere classes is zero modulo two, so evaluating the bundle's $w_2$ gives $r\equiv0\pmod2$. Since $1\le r\le3$, only I remains.

Finally suppose an order-$m$ interval is disjoint from an isolated $(1,1)$ vertex. A tube about its inverse image $A_m$ and the isolated-orbit tube have a common boundary diffeomorphic to $S^2\times S^3$. The normal characters of $A_m$ have absolute values one. Set $u=1$, $v=\pm1$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:normal}. The choice $v=1$ has Euler evaluations $2,0$ and a non-simply-connected unit circle bundle. Hence $v=-1$ and $m\mid2$. Since $m>1$, $m=2$, which is VI. The decomposition used here follows by removing the two disjoint quotient balls and lifting the interval direction on their free complement $S^2\times[0,1]$.
head: environment

label: prop:dihedralfamily
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dihedralfamily}
For each odd $k\ge3$ there is a smooth simply connected $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-manifold with type-VIII graph $(D_k;2,k;2)$ whose underlying manifold is
\[
 E_n=S(\xi_n)\longrightarrow S^4,\qquad
 n=\frac{k^2-1}{8},\qquad p_1(\xi_n)=4n u.
\]
This is a smooth realization and does not assert positive curvature for every $k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the cohomogeneity-one action on $S^4\subset\operatorname{Sym}^2_0(\mathbb R^3)$, with principal isotropy $D_2$ and singular isotropy $K_-,K_+\cong\mathrm O(2)$ about different coordinate axes. Define homomorphisms into a second $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ by multiplying the circle angle by $k$ on $K_-$ and using the ordinary inclusion on $K_+$. Send the reflection in each normalizer to the corresponding half-turn. Because $k$ is odd, the homomorphisms agree on $D_2$. The equivariant principal-bundle construction of Grove--Ziller \cite[Proposition 1.6]{GZ} gives a principal $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ bundle over $S^4$ with a commuting lifted $G$ action. Take its associated two-sphere bundle.

Over the principal base orbit the three axes of $D_2$ give three order-two arcs. At the weight-$k$ end the fiber poles produce a circle orbit with slice $(2,k)$, while the equator produces $D_k$. At the weight-one end the poles give slice $(1,2)$ and the equator has cyclic isotropy. These arcs assemble into the required lollipop; at its $D_k$ vertex the order-$k$ transverse character is $\pm2$.

At the two fixed points of a rotation circle on the base $S^4$, the tangent weights are $(1,2)$ with opposite Euler signs. The associated three-plane fiber weights are $k$ and $1$. Localization gives
\[
 \int_{S^4}p_1(\xi_n)=\frac{k^2-1}{2}=4n.
\]
The total sphere bundle is simply connected by the homotopy sequence. This proves the assertion, and its integral invariants are computed in \eqref{eq:Eninvariants} below.
head: environment

label: lem:noextra
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:noextra}
In cases~(b)--(f), no exceptional stratum occurs other than the interval displayed in~(f). The interior slice is $(1,1)$ in~(c) and~(e), and $(1,2)$ in~(f).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An interior noncyclic finite isotropy group would give an isolated interior stratum. By the boundary-soul theorem it must be the soul. In cases with an interior singular orbit the soul is already that orbit, so such a finite stratum is impossible. In case~(b) there are no eligible boundary endpoints for any exceptional edge, and an exceptional component disjoint from singular strata is excluded by Liu's Proposition~3.6. The same argument applies to~(d), since its boundary fixed-point slices have no exceptional germs.

In~(c) and~(e) all exceptional endpoints would have to be the sole interior singular orbit. With no branching vertex available, an exceptional edge would then close to a loop at that orbit. Both slice weights would be its order, contradicting coprimality. Thus there are no exceptional edges and the two nonzero slice weights have absolute value one. In~(f), the boundary normalizer orbit supplies exactly one order-two germ. It must end at the soul, since a face or a fixed point cannot be an endpoint and there is no other boundary normalizer orbit. A second edge or an additional component would have no possible endpoint except a prohibited loop at the soul. The remaining interior weight is therefore one.
head: environment

label: prop:ballb
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After removing the boundary collar, the principal region is $U=G\times D^3$. Thus
\[
 M=U\cup_WV_k,\qquad W=S(\nu_k)\cong G\times S^2.
\]
For a circle bundle over the simply connected base $F$, the fundamental group of its total space has order equal to the divisibility of its Euler class. Hence $\pi_1(W)=\mathbb Z/2$ forces $k=2n$. Put $c=a+nb$, so $e(\nu_k)=2c$.

The Gysin sequence gives $H^2(W)=\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ and $H^4(W)=\mathbb Z/2$. The torsion generator from $H^2(U)=\mathbb Z/2$ restricts to the class of $c$ modulo $2c$. The restriction $H^3(U)\to H^3(W)$ is an isomorphism, since it restricts as an equivariant degree-one map on a principal $G$ orbit. Mayer--Vietoris now gives torsion-free cohomology in degrees $0,2,4,6$, one generator in each degree, and zero odd cohomology. Generators can be chosen with
\[
 x|_F=c,\qquad y|_F=2ab,\qquad\int_Mxy=1.
\]
For the last normalization, $\operatorname{PD}[F]=2x$ and $\int_Fy|_F=2$ imply $\int_Mxy=1$. Restriction to $F$ is injective in degree four. It follows from $c^2=2nab$ that $x^2=ny$.

Since $TM|_F=TF\oplus\nu_k$, $F$ is spin, and $e(\nu_k)=2c$, restriction gives $w_2(M)|_F=0$. Restriction in degree two modulo two is injective, so $w_2(M)=0$. Moreover $p_1(TF)=0$ and
\[
 p_1(M)|_F=e(\nu_k)^2=8nab=4n\,y|_F,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:Eninvariants}.

Oriented three-plane bundles over $S^4$ are classified by an integer normalized by $p_1(\xi_n)=4n u$ \cite{MS,Husemoller}. Their sphere bundles have exactly \eqref{eq:Eninvariants}: lift the structure group to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ and use its rank-two complex projectivization, or use the vertical Euler class $2x$ and the stable tangent splitting. Wall--Jupp identifies $M$ with $E_n$. The cubic and its integral divisibility distinguish $|n|$; simultaneously changing $x,y$ to $-x,-y$ identifies the systems for $n$ and $-n$.

For existence as a smooth action, the principal $G$ bundle $S(\nu_{2n})\to S^2_b$ has clutching class $2n\bmod2=0$. It can therefore be glued equivariantly to $G\times D^3$. Van Kampen gives simple connectivity, and the local models give exactly the strata in~(b). Automorphisms of the free boundary are absorbed using the free-boundary argument following Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}, together with extension of a sphere diffeomorphism over $D^3$. This proves smooth realizability, with no assertion about strictly positive metrics.
head: environment

label: prop:oddglue
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:oddglue}
The gluing \eqref{eq:Mkdef} exists exactly when $k$ is odd. For each such $k$ it gives a closed simply connected smooth effective $G$-manifold with the complete stratification~(c). The equivariant attaching map introduces no further parameter.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The boundary $W_k=S(\eta\boxtimes L^k)$ is a free $G$-space over $S^2_b$. Local trivializations of $L^k$ show that its principal $G$-bundle clutching class is $k\bmod2$: the transition loop is the weight-$k$ rotation loop in $T\subset G$. On the other side,
\[
 \partial U^G_{1,1}=G\times_TS^3\longrightarrow S^3/T=S^2
\]
is the extension of the Hopf circle bundle along $T\to G$. Its clutching class is the nonzero element of $\pi_1(G)=\mathbb Z/2$. Therefore an equivariant boundary identification exists precisely for odd $k$.

For odd $k$, the Euler class $2a+kb$ is primitive and $W_k$ is simply connected. Both disk-bundle pieces in \eqref{eq:Mkdef} are simply connected, so van Kampen gives $\pi_1(M_k)=0$. The principal isotropy is trivial, and the stated slices contain no further exceptional strata. To compare two attaching maps, compose one with the inverse of the other on $\partial U^G_{1,1}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:extension} absorbs this boundary automorphism into that tube. This proves uniqueness for the fixed normal-bundle data.
head: environment

label: thm:Mk
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Integral classification of the odd family

title: Proof
body_md:
The boundary is $S^2\times S^3$. In Mayer--Vietoris, the map $H^2(U)\to H^2(W_k)$ is an isomorphism, so restriction $H^2(M_k)\to H^2(F)$ is an isomorphism. The remaining terms give $H^3(M_k)=0$ and a short exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow H^4(M_k)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0.
\]
Poincar\'e duality completes the additive computation. The restriction of $TM_k$ to $F$ and the normal Euler class give $w_2=\bar y$ and $\operatorname{PD}[F]=2x+ky$.

The full cubic requires more than restriction to $F$, since $H^4(M_k)\to H^4(F)$ is not injective. We compute it by the localization theorem \cite{AB,BV}. Let $u$ generate $H^2(BT;\mathbb Q)$ for the intrinsic rotation circle in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. The fixed set consists of two copies $F_+,F_-$ of $S^2_b$ over the boundary and two points $q_+,q_-$ on the interior orbit. For the canonical rational $G$-equivariant lifts, the restrictions are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccccc@{}}
\toprule
 & $F_+$ & $F_-$ & $q_+$ & $q_-$\\
\midrule
$x$ & $u/2$ & $-u/2$ & $ku/2$ & $-ku/2$\\
$y$ & $b$ & $b$ & $-u$ & $u$\\
Euler class & $u(u+kb)$ & $u(u-kb)$ & $u^3$ & $-u^3$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The point restrictions follow from the boundary relation $2a+kb=0$ in $H^2(W_k)$ and the fact that the two Weyl-related points have opposite restrictions. The point Euler sign is fixed by integrating the degree-four class $u^2y$: its total integral is zero. Thus these signs do not require an arbitrary extra orientation choice.

For clarity, the contributions from the two surfaces and from the two points, respectively, are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}crr@{}}
\toprule
Class & Surfaces & Points\\
\midrule
$x^3$ & $-k/4$ & $k^3/4$\\
$x^2y$ & $1/2$ & $-k^2/2$\\
$xy^2$ & $0$ & $k$\\
$y^3$ & $0$ & $-2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Their sums give \eqref{eq:Mkcubic}. At $F_\pm$ the equivariant Pontryagin class is $2u^2\pm2kub$, and at $q_\pm$ it is $3u^2$. The surface contributions to $p_1x,p_1y$ are $0,4$, while the point contributions are $3k,-6$. This proves \eqref{eq:Mkp1}. The formulas also verify directly
\[
 \int_M(2x+ky)x^2=0,\quad
 \int_M(2x+ky)xy=1,\quad
 \int_M(2x+ky)y^2=0,
\]
which are the restrictions to $F$.

The discriminant of the binary cubic $\int_M(sx+ty)^3$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mkdisc}
 \Delta_k=-27(k^2-1).
\end{equation}
It is unchanged by an integral change of basis or reversal of the ambient orientation. Hence a diffeomorphism forces $|k|=|\ell|$. Conversely, reversing the orientation of $S^2_b$ identifies the normal data with $k$ replaced by $-k$; the corresponding boundary change is absorbed by Lemma~\ref{lem:extension}. This gives $M_k\cong M_{-k}$. Equivalently, the full systems \eqref{eq:Mkcubic}--\eqref{eq:Mkp1} can be compared by Wall--Jupp. Finally \eqref{eq:Mkdef} is a double disk-bundle decomposition with $b_2=2$, so \cite[Theorem A]{DGGK} proves rational ellipticity.
head: environment

label: lem:balllinks
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:balllinks}
At an isolated $G$-fixed point with tangent representation $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3$, the quotient link is the round hemisphere $S^2_+(1/2)$. At an interior orbit with slice $(1,1)$ it is $S^2(1/2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every invariant inner product on $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3$ is carried to the standard inner product by an equivariant linear isometry. For the standard one write a representative of $S^5/\mathrm{SO}(3)$ as
\[
 z=e^{i\theta}(\cos t\,e_1+i\sin t\,e_2),\qquad
 0\le t\le\pi/4,\quad\theta\in\mathbb R/\pi\mathbb Z.
\]
Projecting the coordinate derivatives perpendicular to the orbits gives
\[
 dt^2+\cos^2(2t)\,d\theta^2
 =\tfrac14(d\rho^2+\sin^2\rho\,d\phi^2),
 \qquad\rho=\pi/2-2t,\quad\phi=2\theta.
\]
The dependent-vector locus is the equator. The second assertion is the ordinary unit Hopf quotient; an invariant Hermitian form on the weight-one $\mathbb C^2$ slice is likewise equivalent to the standard form.
head: environment

label: prop:doublebound
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:doublebound}
Let $f$ count the boundary fixed points of the preceding type and let $r$ count interior singular points. Then $f+2r\le3$. In particular case~(e) cannot occur under \eqref{eq:H}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Compactness gives $\operatorname{sec}_g\ge\kappa>0$. Double $X$ along its whole boundary. Petrunin's theorem \cite{Petrunin} gives curvature at least $\kappa$ on $DX$. Each boundary fixed point contributes one point whose link is the double of $S^2_+(1/2)$, namely $S^2(1/2)$. Each interior singular point contributes two points. Their weighted-Hopf links have three-extent at most $\pi/3$, as recalled in Section~\ref{sec:tools}. The four-point extent inequality therefore gives $f+2r\le3$. In~(e), $f=2$ and $r=1$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:conicpiece
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:conicpiece}
The inverse image $Q$ is a smooth embedded four-manifold equivariantly diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{CP}^2$ with its real $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ action. The interior singular sphere is its complex conic. The oriented normal line has Euler class $\pm h$, where $h$ generates $H^2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb Z)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At the interior endpoint, $Q$ is the weight-two axis plane in the slice $(1,2)$. At the boundary endpoint, it is the standard plane in \eqref{eq:O2slice}. It therefore closes smoothly. Align the principal subgroup as $H=C_2$ about the $z$ axis. At the interior end the singular group is $\mathrm{SO}(2)_z$. At the boundary end it is $\mathrm O(2)_x$, with $x\perp z$: the generator of $H$ lies in the nonidentity component of this normalizer. This relative position, which is not expressed by the abstract symbols $C_2\subset\mathrm O(2)$ alone, is forced by \eqref{eq:O2slice}.

The resulting cohomogeneity-one diagram is the real $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ action on $\mathbb{CP}^2$, with singular orbits $\mathbb{RP}^2$ and the complex conic. The standard cohomogeneity-one classification \cite{Parker,Bredon} gives the equivariant identification. The conic represents twice the projective-line class. Along it the ambient normal plane has circle weight one, and hence Euler number $\pm2$. If $e(\nu Q)=d h$, restriction to the conic gives $2d=\pm2$, so $d=\pm1$.
head: environment

label: lem:cap
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cap}
The complement of an open normal disk bundle of $Q$ is equivariantly diffeomorphic to $D(\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3)$.
head: environment
name: The complementary cap

title: Proof
body_md: Choose the normal tube compatibly with the boundary-soul product description. Its quotient removes a neighborhood of the exceptional interval and leaves a ball with exactly one fixed point and a circle-isotropy side face. Remove a small linear disk about that fixed point. The remaining quotient is a product $D^2\times[0,1]$ with its side-face structure, and there are no other orbit types in it. The interval vector field lifts to a smooth invariant vector field on the corresponding $G$-manifold: on a face chart $\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb C_1$ choose the lift tangent to the face and use the squared normal radius as quotient normal coordinate. The field has no normal component along that face. On principal charts use a connection, and patch these lifts with an invariant partition of unity. Its flow gives an equivariant product cobordism. Thus the outer boundary is obtained from the boundary of the small linear fixed-point disk only by a collar. The small disk has representation $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3$, proving the assertion. This is the smooth equivariant collar argument, not an assumption that an arbitrary topological cap has a standard smoothing.
head: environment

label: thm:matching
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A component of $M^{C_k}$ over the edge is a totally geodesic surface. Its residual rotation-circle action has a horizontal meridian connecting the two singular endpoints. Choose such a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$, perpendicular to the $G$ orbits. Its interior lies over the open edge. The endpoint isotropy circles can be aligned with the unique maximal torus containing $C_k$.

Let $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak{su}(2)\ominus\mathfrak t$. For $A\in\mathfrak m$, write $J_A=A^*|_\gamma$ for the Killing Jacobi field. Its span $P_t$ is the adjoint weight-two plane. At an interior point, the $C_k$ representation on the tangent space is
\[
 \mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb C_2\oplus\mathbb C_s.
\]
Suppose $s\not\equiv\pm2\pmod k$. The weight-two isotypic component is then unique, so parallel transport along the pointwise $C_k$-fixed geodesic preserves $P_t$. Let $Q_0$ be a fixed invariant inner product on $\mathfrak m$. Since $k$ is odd and greater than one, the invariant metric on this real rotation representation is a scalar multiple of $Q_0$. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Jacobilength}
 \langle J_A,J_B\rangle=f(t)^2Q_0(A,B),\qquad f(t)>0.
\end{equation}
In the identifications $A\mapsto J_A$, the derivative operator on this plane is $a(t)\mathrm{id}+b(t)J$, where $J$ is its complex structure. The Wronskian of orbit Jacobi fields vanishes: the Killing identities express it as a multiple of $\langle\gamma',[A^*,B^*]\rangle$, which is zero because the bracket is orbit tangent and $\gamma'$ is horizontal. Thus $b=0$. Differentiating \eqref{eq:Jacobilength} gives $a=f'/f$, whence
\[
 D_tJ_A=(f'/f)J_A,\qquad D_t^2J_A=(f''/f)J_A.
\]
The Jacobi equation now gives, for every nonzero $A$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:concavity}
 K(\gamma',J_A)=-f''/f>0.
\end{equation}

At each endpoint the fields $J_A$ span the noncollapsed tangent plane of the singular sphere, so $f$ extends positively and smoothly to the endpoints. That sphere is totally geodesic. The first-variation formula for its orbit metric in the normal direction $\gamma'$ yields
\[
 f'(0)=f'(L)=0.
\]
This contradicts the strict concavity in \eqref{eq:concavity}. The assumption of inequivalent characters is therefore impossible, proving \eqref{eq:matching}.

At a one-valent vertex on an order-$k$ edge the slice weights are $(1,k)$; its transverse character is one. Thus $1\equiv\pm2\pmod k$. With $k>1$ odd, this forces $k=3$.
head: environment

label: prop:SU2Eunique
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:SU2Eunique}
A $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ action satisfying \eqref{eq:H} with three singular orbits and an exceptional interval is equivariantly diffeomorphic to the commuting right block action on the Eschenburg flag $F_{\mathrm E}$.
head: environment

label: eq:Eschnormal
title: Proof
body_md:
The interval has order three. Its inverse image is
\[
 A_3=G\times_TS(\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb C_3)=\mathbb P(\mathbf 1\oplus L^3)\to S^2,
\]
and the third singular orbit has slice $(1,1)$. The absolute normal characters at the two sections of $A_3$ are both one. Orient the normal line so that the first character is $u=1$. Compatibility in Lemma~\ref{lem:normal} forces the other character to be $v=1$, because $-1\not\equiv1\pmod3$. Consequently its Euler class is one on a section and zero on a fiber. The line is equivariantly
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Eschnormal}
 \nu A_3\cong\rho^*L,
\end{equation}
where $\rho:A_3\to S^2$ is the bundle projection. In induced coordinates its disk bundle is
\[
 G\times_T\bigl(S(\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb C_3)\times D(\mathbb C_1)\bigr).
\]
The unit normal coordinate has weight one, so fixing its phase identifies the boundary equivariantly with $G\times S^2$.

Remove this edge neighborhood and a tube about the remaining singular orbit. The quotient complement is a free $S^2\times[0,1]$ product, and the principal $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ bundle on it is trivial. Absorb it into a collar. The complete manifold is therefore the union of the disk bundle in \eqref{eq:Eschnormal} and $U^G_{1,1}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:extension} absorbs every attaching map on the free boundary. The endpoint characters determine the normal line, so there is a unique equivariant diffeomorphism type with these data. The explicit action verified below realizes this type on $F_{\mathrm E}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Liu's orbit-space dichotomy gives $X\cong S^3$, $B^3$, or $B^4$. If $X\cong S^3$, rational ellipticity is Theorem~A of Khalili Samani--Radeschi \cite{KSR}. The $B^4$ case and the $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ cases with boundary are identified by Liu with $S^6$ or $\mathbb{CP}^3$ \cite[Theorems~1.1--1.2 and~3.1]{LiuCorrected}.

For $G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $X\cong B^3$, Section~\ref{sec:ball} exhausts the configurations. Cases~(a), (d), and~(f) give a sphere or $\mathbb{CP}^3$, and case~(e) is excluded. In case~(b), the fibration $S^2\to E_n\to S^4$ implies rational ellipticity by the rational homotopy exact sequence. In case~(c), the decomposition \eqref{eq:Mkdef} is a double disk bundle with $b_2(M_k)=2$. Theorem~A of DeVito--Galaz-Garc\'ia--Kerin \cite{DGGK} applies: its six-dimensional hypothesis is $b_2\le3$, which is satisfied here. Thus all cases are rationally elliptic.

Liu gives $\chi(M)\in\{2,4,6\}$. A simply connected rationally elliptic space with positive Euler characteristic has no odd-degree rational cohomology \cite{FHT}. Poincar\'e duality now gives $\chi(M)=2+2b_2(M)$. Herrmann's classification of rationally elliptic six-manifolds \cite{Herrmann}, restricted to this Betti range and positive Euler characteristic, yields the six real homotopy types stated in the corollary.
head: environment

label: prop:productCheeger
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:productCheeger}
For either action, let $g_0$ be a $G$-invariant product metric on $S^2\times S^4$. Every diagonal Cheeger deformation $g_s$, $s\ge0$, has a zero-curvature two-plane at every point. No conformal rescaling of any $g_s$ has everywhere positive sectional curvature.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the Cheeger submersion \cite{CheegerNotes}
\[
 \sigma:(M\times G,g_0+s^{-1}Q)\longrightarrow(M,g_s),\qquad
 \sigma(p,a)=a^{-1}p,
\]
where $Q$ is bi-invariant and $s>0$. At $p$ choose $0\ne X\in T S^2$ and $0\ne Y\in T S^4$ orthogonal to the $G$-orbit in the second factor. Such $Y$ exists because those orbits have dimension at most three. Define $L\in\mathfrak g$ by $Q(L,Z)=g_0(X,Z^*)$. At $(p,1)$ the vectors
\[
 \widehat X=(X,-sL),\qquad\widehat Y=(Y,0)
\]
are horizontal. Their ambient curvature numerator is zero: the $M$ components form a mixed product plane and the second $G$ component vanishes.

The O'Neill term also vanishes. The metric-dual one-form $\eta_Z$ of a vertical fundamental field is a sum of forms from $M$ and $G$. Its $M$ part is the sum of one-forms pulled back from the two product factors. Hence $d\eta_Z(\widehat X,\widehat Y)=0$ for every $Z$. For horizontal extensions this implies $[\widehat X,\widehat Y]^{\mathrm{vert}}=0$. O'Neill's horizontal curvature formula \cite{ONeill} therefore gives a zero plane in $(M,g_s)$. The case $s=0$ is immediate.

More generally, suppose a metric $g$ on a compact manifold has a nonpositive plane at every point. At a minimum of a smooth function $f$, its gradient vanishes and its Hessian is nonnegative. The conformal curvature formula \cite{Petersen} gives, for a $g$-orthonormal basis $U,V$ of such a plane,
\[
 K_{e^{2f}g}(U\wedge V)
 =e^{-2f}\bigl(K_g(U\wedge V)-\operatorname{Hess}_gf(U,U)-\operatorname{Hess}_gf(V,V)\bigr)\le0.
\]
Apply this to each $g_s$.
head: environment

label: thm:noTGproduct
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:noTGproduct}
There is no positively curved metric on $S^2\times S^4$ for which either standard product projection is a Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers. No invariance assumption is needed.
head: environment

label: eq:ONmixed
title: Proof
body_md:
We use O'Neill's mixed curvature formula for totally geodesic fibers \cite{ONeill}:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ONmixed}
 K(X,V)=|A_XV|^2
\end{equation}
for horizontal and vertical unit vectors. For the projection onto $S^2$, the linear map $A_X$ sends the four-dimensional vertical space into the one-dimensional horizontal space orthogonal to $X$. It has a nonzero kernel, producing a zero mixed plane.

Consider the projection onto $S^4$. We first show that the two-sphere fibers would necessarily be round; this is not an initial assumption. Totally geodesic fibers are mutually isometric under horizontal transport. The curvature of this transport connection is a vertical Killing field on each fiber, represented, up to the conventional sign and factor, by $2A_XY$. At a point of a fiber, if the values of these Killing fields failed to span its tangent plane, a nonzero vertical $V$ would be perpendicular to all $A_XY$. The identity $\langle A_XV,Y\rangle=-\langle V,A_XY\rangle$ would imply $A_XV=0$ for all $X$, contradicting \eqref{eq:ONmixed}. The fiber isometry group therefore acts transitively. Its Gaussian curvature is constant, and Gauss--Bonnet makes that constant positive. All fibers are isometric round spheres of one radius.

The connection thus reduces to an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ connection on the round sphere bundle. Let $\Omega$ be its curvature, identified fiberwise with a two-form on the base valued in $\mathbb R^3$. At a unit sphere point $p$, the horizontal O'Neill tensor is
\[
 A_XY=-\tfrac12\Omega(X,Y)\times p.
\]
For every nonzero $w\in\mathbb R^3$, the two-form $\Omega_w=\langle\Omega,w\rangle$ on the four-dimensional base must be nondegenerate. Otherwise choose $X\ne0$ in its kernel, $p\perp w$, and the vertical vector $V=w\times p$. Since $p\times V=w$, the displayed formula implies $A_XV=0$, again contradicting positivity. This is the fatness condition for the associated two-sphere bundle.

The standard coupling-form construction for a fat round two-sphere bundle now gives a symplectic form on its total space; see Fine--Panov \cite[Section~2.2]{FinePanov}. We use that theorem directly. In a trivialization its familiar local expression is the fiber area form minus $d\langle p,\gamma\rangle$, with $\gamma$ the connection one-form, and nondegeneracy is precisely the condition on $\Omega_w$ above. But
\[
 H^2(S^2\times S^4;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R\alpha,\qquad\alpha^2=0.
\]
Every degree-two class has zero cube, whereas a symplectic form on a closed six-manifold has nonzero cubic integral. This contradiction proves the theorem.
head: environment

label: prop:additional
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:additional}
For the action \eqref{eq:SO3productaction}, a positively curved invariant metric cannot extend to the diagonal $\mathrm O(3)$ action. Moreover no nonidentity standard transformation
\[
 (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x,y,Rz),\qquad R\in\mathrm O(2),
\]
can be an isometry of a positively curved metric on $M$.
For \eqref{eq:SU2productaction}, a positively curved invariant metric cannot also be invariant under the full commuting right-$\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ action on $q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fixed components of isometries are totally geodesic. We apply Wilking's connectedness theorem \cite{WilkingConnected}: a closed codimension-$k$ totally geodesic submanifold of a positively curved $n$-manifold has $(n-2k+1)$-connected inclusion.

A reflection in the diagonal $\mathrm O(3)$ action fixes $S^1\times S^3$, of codimension two. Its inclusion would be three-connected, contradicting its nontrivial fundamental group. A nonidentity rotation of the suspension coordinates fixes $S^2\times S^2$, also of codimension two. Its second homotopy group has rank two, whereas $\pi_2(M)$ has rank one. A reflection of the suspension coordinates fixes $S^2\times S^3$, of codimension one. Five-connectedness would identify its $\pi_3\cong\mathbb Z^2$ with $\pi_3(M)\cong\mathbb Z$, again impossible.

For the quaternionic action, adjoining right-$\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ makes the action cohomogeneity one: the regular orbits are the level sets of $t$. Verdiani's classification of positively curved, even-dimensional, simply connected cohomogeneity-one manifolds \cite{Verdiani}, also discussed in \cite{GWZ}, would make $M$ a compact rank-one symmetric space. The integral cohomology ring of $S^2\times S^4$ excludes this possibility.
head: environment

label: prop:boundaryidentity
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply the standard warped-product curvature formulas to \eqref{eq:boundarywarped}, and then the Gauss equation \cite{Petersen}. The pure blocks of the second fundamental form vanish by \eqref{eq:IIblocks}. The remaining Gauss correction on a mixed plane is $+|\mathrm{II}(U,X)|^2$, which is \eqref{eq:boundarybeta}.
head: environment

label: cor:boundaryobstruction
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The pointwise inequalities follow directly from Proposition~\ref{prop:boundaryidentity}. At a minimum the Hessian is nonnegative, so $\mathcal S>0$ forces injectivity of $\beta$. A globally injective $\beta:TS^2\to S^2\times\mathbb C$ would trivialize $TS^2$, contradicting its Euler number two. Hence $\beta$ degenerates somewhere, ruling out constant $f$. Tracing $\mathcal S>0$ and integrating gives \eqref{eq:boundaryenergy}, since
\[
 \int_B f^{-1}\Delta_h f\,dA_h=
 \int_B f^{-2}|df|_h^2\,dA_h.
\]
The quantitative assertion follows by tracing the lower bound $\mathcal S\ge\kappa h$.
head: environment

label: prop:boundarycompatible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:boundarycompatible}
There are smooth data $(h,f,\beta)$ on $B=S^2$ satisfying all the inequalities in \eqref{eq:boundarynecessary}. They occur as the induced metric and mixed second fundamental form along $F$ for a smooth invariant metric on $M$. This assertion does not give positive curvature on all ambient planes.
head: environment

label: eq:boundarydata
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $b=(b_1,b_2,r)\in S^2$, $\zeta=b_1+ib_2$, and choose $0<\varepsilon\le\tfrac12$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundarydata}
 h=g_{S^2(1)},\qquad f=1-\varepsilon r,\qquad
 \beta=\sqrt\varepsilon\bigl((1+r)d\zeta-\zeta\,dr\bigr).
\end{equation}
These are globally smooth. Direct calculation gives
\[
 \beta^*\beta=\varepsilon(1+r)^2h,
 \qquad \operatorname{Hess}_hf=\varepsilon r h,
 \qquad |df|_h\le\varepsilon<1.
\]
Thus
\[
 \mathcal S=\varepsilon\left((1+r)^2-\frac{r}{1-\varepsilon r}\right)h>0.
\]
For $r<0$ both contributions are nonnegative and their sum is positive. For $0\le r\le1$, the expression in parentheses is at least $(1+r)^2-2r=1+r^2$. Also $K_h=1$. The degeneracy of $\beta$ is at the maximum of $f$, not at its minimum.

To realize these tensors, equip $E=\operatorname{pr}_1^*TS^2\to F$ with its standard fiber metric and an invariant connection. Prescribe $g_F=f^2g_{S^2}+h$ and let $\mathrm{II}$ have the pure blocks \eqref{eq:IIblocks} and, for an orbit coordinate vector $u\in T_xS^2$, mixed block
\[
 \mathrm{II}(u,X)=f\bigl(\operatorname{Re}\beta(X)u+
               \operatorname{Im}\beta(X)J_xu\bigr)\in E_{(x,b)}.
\]
In an equivariant tubular neighborhood, set for small $n\in E_p$
\[
 g_n(A^h,B^h)=g_F(A,B)-2\langle\mathrm{II}(A,B),n\rangle,
\]
use the Euclidean metric in the fiber directions, and make horizontal and vertical directions orthogonal. Compactness gives a uniform neighborhood on which this tensor is positive definite. Its normal derivative at the zero section realizes the prescribed second fundamental form. An invariant cutoff and a convex interpolation with any invariant metric extend it to all of $M$ without changing it near $F$.

The planes in Proposition~\ref{prop:boundaryidentity} consequently have positive curvature along $F$. Curvatures of planes containing normal vectors, general oblique planes, and planes in the regular part have not been controlled. This is exactly the limitation of the construction.
head: environment

label: prop:firstvariation
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:firstvariation}
Let $g_s$ be a smooth family of metrics on $S^2\times S^4$ with $g_0$ the round product metric. If the first variation of sectional curvature is nonnegative on every initially mixed plane, it vanishes on every such plane. In particular this vanishing is necessary if $\operatorname{sec}_{g_s}>0$ for every sufficiently small $s>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The product of a great circle in each sphere is a flat totally geodesic torus $T$ for $g_0$. Its second fundamental form for $g_s$ is $O(s)$, so its quadratic Gauss correction is $O(s^2)$. The first variation of its intrinsic Gaussian curvature therefore equals that of the ambient sectional curvature on $TT$. Differentiating Gauss--Bonnet gives
\[
 \int_T\left.\frac{d}{ds}\right|_{0}K_{g_s}(T_pT)\,dA_{g_0}=0,
\]
since the initial curvature is zero. A nonnegative integrand must vanish identically. Every mixed plane is tangent to a torus of this form. Positivity for $s>0$ implies nonnegativity of the right derivative at zero, proving the last assertion.
head: environment
